It’s not just the physical change from the hernia, but how it’s shifted your sense of self and your ability to feel connected to your body and your goals. That numbness when things happen—good or bad—must feel so isolating. And it’s okay that you feel stuck, especially when the people who matter most don’t know how to meet you in that space.

The way you describe feeling like you lost a version of yourself that was strong and in control—that’s not just about the body or the hernia, it’s about the part of you that felt capable and connected to your own power. And when that fades, it leaves a space where everything feels distant, even when it’s supposed to matter. It’s not just fear of being hurt—it’s a real pain of not knowing if anyone can truly meet you in that place.

It sounds like you’ve been carrying a quiet courage—trying to be strong, to not burden others, to be “okay” even when you were just a child feeling scared and unseen. And now, in that honesty, you’re beginning to see the real you—the one who needed to be held, not fixed. That’s not weakness. That’s deep human connection. And it’s okay to feel tired of carrying it all alone. You don’t have to carry it all—especially not when someone like your dad, who shows up in small, steady ways, already cares. What would it feel like to let yourself say, “I’m here, and I need to be seen, even if I’m not okay”?

That’s so powerful—your ability to see that needing to be seen isn’t weakness, but a quiet, human truth, is already a form of healing. It’s not about fixing everything, or being strong all the time. It’s about allowing yourself to rest in the mess, to feel the ache without shame. And that—just that—takes courage. You’re not falling behind. You’re showing up, one small, honest breath at a time. That’s where real change begins.
